Name: Kodai Senga
Report: After starting his career as a reliever, Senga moved into the Fukuoka Hawks rotation in 2017 and has spent the last half decade as one of the better starters (and hardest-throwing pitchers) in all of NPB. While the 29-year-old righty struggled with walks early in his tenure as a starter (he walked 75 hitters in 180 innings in 2019 and 57 hitters in 121 innings in ‘20), free passes have become less of an issue during the last two seasons. Senga’s walk rate fell from the 10-11% range to the 8-8.5% range during that stretch, and his WHIP was a measly 1.05. Senga has added four ticks to his fastball since debuting in NPB. This wasn't a gradual increase, either – it happened all at once in 2019. He now sits 96 mph and will touch as high as 102, though he typically tops out at 99 in any given start. Even though premium velocity is rare in Japan, Senga’s fastball doesn't play like a premium pitch due to its shape and angle. In fact, his dastardly mid-80s splitter, which falls off the table and finishes below the strike zone, is easily his best offering, garnering twice as many swings and misses as his fastball in 2022, and about as many whiffs as the rest of his many pitches combined. Those pitches (in order of usage) are a cutter, slider, and the occasional curveball, all bending in anywhere between 94 and 75 mph, with the slider’s shape and velo sometimes bleeding into the other two. While his breaking ball command is inconsistent, Senga’s velocity, splitter, repertoire depth, and demonstrated durability make him a fit as no. 3 or 4 starter on a contender like the Mets, who signed him to a five-year, $75 million deal.

Name: Masataka Yoshida
Report:
Yoshida has been on The Board for over a year now, and he was originally evaluated in a way that pegged him as a fun part-time weapon (we compared him to Lenny Harris) rather than the $100 million player the Boston Red Sox believe him to be. Shortly before publication, the Red Sox signed Yoshida to a five-year, $90 million contract and paid an additional $15.4 million posting fee to the Orix Buffaloes. That's the kind of contract you give to a 2-WAR player, a hitter who exists in the middle third of MLB's corner outfield talent hierarchy. Is it possible that the little Yoshida, all 5-foot-8, 176 pounds of him, can thump with that contingent? In his own way, yes. While Yoshida's skill set is shaped in an extreme hit-over-power style atypical of a big league corner outfielder, there are others who have had success with similarly tailored talent, most especially Steven Kwan and Jeff McNeil, with the likes of Tony Kemp and Jurickson Profar providing a look at the bottom of what an acceptable range of performance outcomes for Yoshida would be. 
This guy can hit. Yoshida is a career .327/.421/.539 hitter in NPB with more career walks than strikeouts, and the last two seasons, he's actually walked twice as often as he's K'd. He has been almost impossible to strike out in Japan, and his feel for contact is superlative enough that even though he's not very physical and is a left field-only guy, he's arguably elite at the game's most important skill. His ability to maneuver the barrel around the zone by altering not only his hands but also the overall posture of his body is very special, and there isn't a spot in the strike zone where Yoshida can't make contact with the baseball. He can drop the bat head to golf out middle-in mistakes and get extended on fastballs up and away from him to do doubles damage the opposite way. While Yoshida is such an explosive rotator for his size that his bat often strikes the ground behind him at the end of his follow through, he hits the ball on the ground a lot, and his GB% has been in the 47-51% range for the last six seasons. Opposing pitchers can limit his ability to do damage by working him with soft stuff down and away, but Yoshida is still going to find a way to put the ball in play. His measly 5% swinging strike rate was seventh-best among qualified NPB hitters in 2022 and only one of the hitters ahead of him could muster more than three homers, while Yoshida yanked out 21. Among the best contact hitters in NPB, Yoshida is separating himself with how much power he's getting to. 
Will some version of this hold up against MLB pitching? When you isolate Yoshida's performance against hard fastballs, you start to get a better idea of how things might look over here. Versus fastballs 93 mph and above (202 pitches), Yoshida hit .273/.333/.455; against 94 mph and up (153 pitches), he hit .279/.340/.395; and against 95 mph (88 pitches) and above, his line was .296/.345/.370 (all of this is from Synergy Sports). Anything more than that and the sample gets too small to be meaningful, and it's possible 88 pitches already is. You can see the dip in his SLG within that sample but the good news is Yoshida maintains about a 5-to-1 ball-in-play to whiff ratio within all three of those velo bands. The hit tool is going to translate and Yoshida's plate discipline probably will, too. His 23% O-Swing% would put him among the majors' 10 most selective outfielders. The contact/OBP combo should enable him to produce in the 1.5 to 2 WAR range, similar to the last couple seasons of Andrew Benintendi or a more patient Alex Verdugo. It's possible that the amount and quality of contact Yoshida makes gives him a higher power ceiling than we anticipate.

Name: Ethan Salas
Report: The brother of Marlins prospect Jose Salas, Ethan has been seen and known about for about as long as it's possible for a player this age to be known, having competed in half a dozen Perfect Game events dating back to 2017. He's one of the best players from what will now be the 2023 signing class. Salas is a sweet-swinging, lefty-hitting catcher with baby soft defensive hands, and an ultra-quick release behind the dish. His swing is very balanced and rhythmic, and he can shorten up to hit stuff toward the top of the zone. Initially Salas looked like a hit-over-power prospect, but as he's maturing, he's becoming more explosive. The risk on teenage catching is extreme, but Salas is very gifted and has star-level ceiling. He's expected to get one of the class' biggest bonuses, close to $4 million.

Name: Brandon Mayea
Report: Mayea derives his power from precise, flush contact. Though somewhat more physically mature than most prospects his age, he isn't especially big and strong, nor projectable. He simply has great feel for contact and swings with rotational verve, and the combination is enough to punish the baseball. Short levers and prodigious bat control help drive impact hit tool projection, while his posture through contact creates natural swing loft that indicates he'll get to whatever power he ends up growing into. Additionally, Mayea looks poised to stay up the middle of the diamond due to his speed, defensive instincts, and medium build. This makes him an exceptional, well-rounded prospect for his age. Industry sources indicate Mayea and the Yankees have a verbal agreement for just shy of $5 million.

Name: Felnin Celesten
Report: A well-rounded switch hitter with a gorgeous swing and some pull pop, Celesten is an exciting shortstop prospect whose actions make him likely to stay at the position. He's been at or near the top of his age group for a couple of years and is likely to receive a bonus in the $4.5 million range when eligible to sign.

Name: Joendry Vargas
Report: Vargas' combination of physical projection and switch-hitting ability is the most exciting since amateur Ronny Mauricio, and Vargas is similarly built and surprisingly deft with the barrel from both sides of the plate. Where he deviates from Mauricio is on defense, where Vargas tends to play high, and at his size, he is likely to move off of short and perhaps off the infield altogether. He is a rare and exceptional offensive prospect with a cathedral's ceiling.

Name: Welbyn Francisca
Report: Perhaps the most entertaining hitter on this list, Francisca is a switch-hitting bat control savant. He can alter his footwork and bat path to put the barrel on just about anything. Arm strength may limit him to second base, but the bat is the carrying tool here. He's not getting as much money as lots of the other players in the class, but Francisca's switch-hitting and up-the-middle fit make him one of its better all-around profiles.

Name: Luis Guanipa
Report: Guanipa's combination of bat and foot speed is very exciting, as he has a chance to both hit for power and be an impact center field defender. Rhythmic and explosive, the ball comes off Guanipa's bat with shocking force for an athlete his size. Because he's quite compact, he lacks traditional power projection but visual evaluations of his hitting hands still generate optimism in this regard. He could be a very dangerous big league leadoff hitter. Rival clubs indicate the Braves and Guanipa have a verbal agreement just south of $3 million.

Name: Hendry Chivilli
Report: The scintillating Chivilli has a long-levered, projectable frame, runs a 6.5 60-yard dash, has a 70-grade arm, and also has exciting bat speed. He's also shown a relatively mature two-strike approach in games, and tracks pitches well. As well-rounded as he is exciting, Chivilli is said to have a verbal deal with Minnesota at just over $2 million.

Name: Alfredo Duno
Report: Duno has perhaps the best bat speed on this entire list, and he has a Gary Sánchez-ish present toolset. Not a slam dunk to stay at catcher, Duno projects to be a 40- or 45-grade receiver and has a plus-plus arm. He had some issues hitting in games while some of our notes on him were being collected, and recent reports are arguably less useful because Duno is now much more physical than the players he competes against at workouts. He has gigantic, 30-homer ceiling, which would make him an impact big league catcher if he can stay back there. The rate of attrition for teenage catchers and for players with hit tool risk is high; Duno is both.

Name: Jesus Starlyn Caba
Report: Caba is an electric infield athlete with plus-plus footwork, hands, and a plus arm, perhaps the best defender in the January 2023 international class. His swing will likely be refined as he adds strength through maturation, but he's shown promising hand-eye coordination to this point. His verbal deal with Philadelphia is thought to be for about $3 million.

Name: Brailer Guerrero
Report: Guerrero has one of the most picturesque swings in the 2023 international class, a lovely and dynamic cut that produces all-fields power. At his size, he is a certain corner outfielder, but his hitting talent makes him a potential everyday force.

Name: Enmanuel Bonilla
Report: The burly Bonilla already has rare power for a prospect his age, and it is weaponized by very advanced feel to hit. A scout with awareness of its gravity put a Manny Ramirez swing comp on Bonilla. There's a chance his frame gets to a LF/DH area because he's already so physical, but Bonilla looks like a potential middle-of-the-order force.

Name: Luis Danys Morales
Report: The timing of Morales' defection from the Cuban U-23 national team (it was summer of 2021) meant only teams that had yet to commit bonus pool space could make him a competitive offer. It may have been a seller's market, though, as it seems more teams than usual had (and still have) about $2 million in space remaining. It meant Oakland's offer had to approach $3 million (as reported by Cuban journalist Francys Romero) to get clear of other clubs. The A's often have late-market money remaining and have used it on late-market Cuban players to mixed results. Morales was a known prospect well before he defected and even pitched a little bit in Series Nacional, working with a fastball/curveball combination there. In post-departure workouts he would sit 94-98 mph with upshot angle and riding life on a fastball that leads a four-pitch mix. While his arm action is a little long, Morales' delivery is otherwise athletic, explosive, and beautiful. He has a perfect pitcher's build at a broad-shouldered 6-foot-3 and presents Oakland with a malleable, exciting collection of abilities that project into the middle of a rotation eventually.

Name: Derniche Valdez
Report: While he's only of medium build, Valdez is one of the better infield athletes in the 2023 class, as is apparent in his infield feet and actions as well as the way his lower half works throughout his swing. While he's on the smaller side, Valdez does not get cheated at the plate and has a huge, flexible stride that coaxes more power than you'd expect from his little frame. He is quite like Rangers prospect Luisangel Acuña in this way.

Name: Camilo Diaz
Report: Looking for elite bat speed? Diaz comes close, his hips and torso turning like the head of an owl in the blink of an eye. While Diaz rotates as fast as anyone in his class, he does so with some mechanical flaws and shortcuts that make his hit tool feel flimsy. Scouts who combine this with a third base projection tend to be lower on him, but if Diaz can refine his barrel feel without sacrificing bat speed, it won't matter where he ends up playing defense. Originally rumored to be headed to Texas for $3 million, Diaz is now rumored to have an agreement with Houston for closer to $2.5 million.

Name: Rainel Arias
Report: In keeping with the Giants' style of signing international prospects, Arias is in the Luciano/Canario vein: he swings incredibly hard for a player his age, and already has the ability to put balls out to right/center field and do big damage with conservative footwork. Scouts see Arias in the traditional right field mold, with power-over-hit skillset on offense, the chance to grow into more raw thump, and a plus arm.

Name: Sebastian Walcott
Report: Walcott was seen some in the U.S. during the fall of 2021 and leapt off the field because of his physicality and power. He looks like a future NFL tight end in his uniform and has the kind of pull power you'd expect from a prospect built like that. He has some crude-looking but effective feel to hit and can bend at the waist to poke outer-half stuff the other way, but Walcott's bat isn't in the hitting zone for very long and his breaking ball recognition during those stateside games was poor. Walcott is a balletic and graceful infield defender, which is incredible to watch at his size, and he might be a plus third base defender at peak. He's a high-risk hit tool prospect with huge power upside.

Name: Kevin Ereu
Report: One of the more polished all-around players in the class, Ereu has plus infield footwork and actions, and is physical enough to threaten the gaps on offense. He looks like a third round West Coast college infielder in his skills and build, and is perceived to have a high floor.

Name: Yoeilin Cespedes
Report: Stocky and strong, Cespedes is FanGraphs' favorite flavor of prospect: a compact middle infielder with a water-carrying hit tool. His size limits his power projection and he may end up a Yonny Hernandez-type of utilityman, especially if he can't stick at shortstop, but Cespedes could end up with enough stick to be an everyday man at the keystone.

Name: Gian Zapata
Report: Among the most physically projectable athletes in the 2023 class, Zapata is a typical Diamondbacks international prospect in the Alvin Guzman mold. You can dream on how much power Zapata will grow into while also hoping that he'll stay in center field, though his rocket arm will be an asset in right if he eventually has to move.

Name: Ariel Castro
Report: Built like an NFL cornerback, the sinewy Castro generates real pull-side thunder with his hands, and does so in a short distance. He's not an especially loose athlete or rotator, but his combination of present power and body projection make him a high-ceiling corner outfield prospect.

Name: Junior Arias
Report: The lanky, broad-shouldered Arias has a chance to grow into big power. His swing has less verve than those of his peers, but Arias' feel to hit is pretty good despite his medium twitch. Scouts who think the bat speed will arrive as part of Arias' athletic development like him most, as that would give him the hit/power combination to profile in right field (his arm is plus).

Name: Yerlin Luis
Report: The diminutive Luis swings harder than you'd expect given his size, and he has precocious feel for the barrel. While he lacks the typical frame-based power projection of an international outfield prospect, his hit tool may be good enough for him to outperform his raw power in games.

Name: Andy Acevedo
Report: A hitterish little lefty stick, Acevedo's polished hit tool drives an otherwise vanilla corner outfield profile. He might hit enough to be a good everyday player depite the middling other tools.

Name: Reiner Lopez
Report: Lopez's closest body comp is to Pelicans forward Brandon Ingram, who Lopez is only an inch shorter than at age 16 (my sources have him listed at 6-foot-7). There's a real possibility that Lopez reaches 7-feet tall by the time he's done growing. He is shockingly graceful and athletic for a pitcher his size, and even though we're currently talking about a prospect throwing 87-89 mph and peaking around 93, there are reasons to project on Lopez's arm strength that we hope are obvious.

Name: Emil Valencia
Report: He's going to have to rake since it appears his best defensive fit is in left field, but Valencia's lovely swing might enable that. He is short to the ball, track pitches very well, moves the barrel all over the zone, and is strong enough to do damage. Simply one of the most polished hitters in the class, Valencia is purported to have a verbal deal with Houston.

Name: Jun-seok Shim
Report: Shim skipped the KBO draft in order to sign with an MLB club right away, and reports in Korean media suggest he'll head to the U.S. in January to work out. He's a big, physically-mature righty with huge present arm strength, creeping into the upper-90s. His slow, mid-70s curveball is easy to identify out of his hand but it has lovely shape and depth of break, so perhaps it can be sculpted into a more traditional big league breaking ball. Opinions around Shim vary because he offers less physical projection than is typical in this market, even for an older pitcher. A source with a Korean club indicated to FanGraphs that they consider Pittsburgh the favorites to sign Shim, though that is less certain than the other projections made for the international amateur market on this site.

Name: Daiverson Gutierrez
Report: Sometimes prospects change during the time between when a team and player have a verbal agreement and when the player actually signs. There are ops personnel and agents who think Gutierrez has gotten quite big, quite quickly in the months leading up to actually signing, but it hasn't changed where he fits on defense and it could change again in a short amount of time because his career has just begun. He is otherwise a typically exciting teenage catching prospect with a plus arm and potential plus raw power.

Name: Ludwig Espinoza
Report: A glove-first utility type, Espinosa is a true shortstop with precocious feel to hit.

Name: Jeremy Rodriguez
Report: Slick and smooth on defense, Rodriguez has a well-composed medium frame and a balanced, compact swing. He's a well-rounded prospect without a premium tool.

Name: Arnaldo Lantigua
Report: A gigantic-framed youngster with exciting rotational athleticism and power potential, Lantigua is a typical corner outfield power prospect thanks to his physical projection.

Name: Tony Ruiz
Report: Another huge-framed corner outfield prospect with exciting power potential, Ruiz's frame and swing are reminiscent of Nick Castellanos.

Name: Robert Galaz
Report: This player's name appears in a multitude of different ways: Robert Calaz, Robert Gala and, as initially dictated to FanGraphs by a scouting source, Robert Galaz. We'll update if necessary when his signing (our sources: Colorado for about $2.7 million) is made official. Galaz is a huge power-hitting prospect with plus pull-side pop. He's a bit lumbering and, when that's combined with his size, is toward the very bottom of this class' long-term defensive projection. He'll be developed as a corner outfielder; the DH designation here is more to indicate we think that's in play for him rather than his immediate position.

Name: Janero Miller
Report: A two-way prospect with exciting tools, Miller has been seen often in the U.S. (usually at tournaments in Florida) and is expected to sign with Miami. He's a projectable switch-hitter with crude feel for the barrel and the speed to be developed in center field, while on the mound he's peaking in the low-90s and has a slow, shapely breaking ball. He's a deep projection prospect likely to get a mid-six-figure bonus from the Marlins.
